subsection: 10. Culture and religion: national identity, the literature of WWI, church–state tensions and anti-Semitism, 1871–1920

notes.h: Nationalism and national identity in the arts
notes.b: Nationalism is loyalty to the nation and the belief that each nation should be united, strong and self-governing. Between 1871 and 1914 artists turned that belief into music, buildings and poetry, which is why culture matters in the story of the nation states.
points: Cultural nationalism used history, myth, folk tradition (the songs and tales of ordinary country people), language and landscape to prove that a people had a distinct identity, so a nation's art became evidence for its right to exist.

There were two kinds. Established, imperial states such as Germany and Britain used culture to express pride and power. Peoples without their own state, such as the Czechs, Finns and Norwegians, used it to assert an identity that their rulers did not recognise.

Across Europe, governments and nationalist societies spread national identity by founding national museums, galleries and theatres, teaching national history in schools and fostering national languages, so ordinary people absorbed it as well as artists.
Pre-1914 cultural nationalism fed the patriotic mood of 1914, because a generation had grown up taught that the nation deserved loyalty and sacrifice. It also shaped the idealistic early war poetry.
notes.tip: Examiners want at least four examples from different countries, each tied to the nation it expressed and to its political situation (stateless or imperial), and a link to the patriotism of 1914.

notes.h: Established and imperial states: Wagner, monuments, Elgar and Kipling
notes.b: In Germany and Britain, nationalist culture celebrated a state that already existed and was powerful. It turned myth, history and empire into sources of pride.
points: Richard Wagner built his operas on Germanic myth, so they presented the Germans as heirs to an ancient heroic tradition. His Ring cycle (Der Ring des Nibelungen) was first staged in full at his own Bayreuth theatre in August 1876.

Wagner died in Venice in 1883, but the Bayreuth Festival continued under his widow Cosima as a shrine of German culture. His anti-Jewish essay 'Judaism in Music' (1850, republished under his name in 1869) links him to the anti-Semitism of the age.

The Hermann Monument in the Teutoburg Forest, completed in 1875, honours Arminius (Hermann), the Germanic leader who defeated three Roman legions in AD 9. The new Reich thus claimed a heroic ancestry of resistance to foreign rule.
The Monument to the Battle of the Nations at Leipzig was unveiled in 1913, the centenary of Napoleon's defeat there in 1813, so it tied German identity to the memory of a national victory.

Edward Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 (1901) supplied the tune for 'Land of Hope and Glory' in the Coronation Ode (1902), with words by A. C. Benson. Together they expressed British imperial confidence, for example in the praise of a great Empire.
Rudyard Kipling, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1907, celebrated British soldiers and the Empire in Recessional (1897, refrain 'Lest we forget') and The White Man's Burden (1899).

Kipling's only son John was killed at the Battle of Loos in 1915. Kipling later worked for the Imperial War Graves Commission and chose the inscription 'Their Name Liveth for Evermore', so his life links imperial pride to the grief of the war.
notes.tip: Keep the distinction clear: Elgar and Kipling wrote for an imperial power, while Smetana and Sibelius wrote for peoples ruled by empires. Wagner died in 1883, so Bayreuth after that date is his legacy.

notes.h: Peoples without a state: Smetana, Sibelius and Grieg
notes.b: For peoples ruled by an empire, music could say what politics forbade. Composers drew on their own history, landscape and folk tunes to show that the nation existed.
points: Bedřich Smetana's Má vlast ('My Country'), six symphonic poems (orchestral pieces that tell a story or paint a scene) composed in 1874-79, includes Vltava ('The Moldau'). It celebrated Bohemian history and landscape when Bohemia was part of Austria-Hungary and the Czechs sought more autonomy.

Jean Sibelius's Finlandia (1899, revised 1900) was written for a protest against Russian censorship of the Finnish press. Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, so the piece became a symbol of Finnish resistance to Russification (imposing Russian language and control on minorities).

Edvard Grieg wrote incidental music (music played during a play) for Henrik Ibsen's Peer Gynt, first performed in 1876, using the Norwegian folk idiom. Norway was in union with Sweden until 1905, so the music expressed a distinct Norwegian identity.
Because these peoples had no state of their own, culture was often their main means of proving they were a nation, which made art a form of political resistance.
notes.tip: When you give an example, name the nation and its political situation: Czechs inside Austria-Hungary, Finns under Russia, Norwegians in union with Sweden.

notes.h: The literature of World War I: why attitudes changed
notes.b: War writing is best understood as a story of changing attitudes: patriotic idealism in 1914-15, then disillusionment, anger and pity, then a disenchanted post-war view. The reasons lie in how the war was fought.
points: On the Western Front (the line of trenches across France and Belgium), trench deadlock, gas, shelling and huge casualties from 1915 turned the hope of a short heroic war into years of mass death.
The Battle of the Somme (1 July to November 1916) shows the scale: on its first day the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties, about 19,000 of them dead.
Writers also felt a gap between home-front propaganda, which kept praising glory, and what soldiers experienced, so much later writing is angry at those who had not been there.

Censorship limited what soldiers could say in letters and the press. It did not stop protest being published during the war, because Le Feu appeared in 1916 and Sassoon's statement and The Old Huntsman in 1917.

In short, there are three phases: patriotic idealism (1914-15), disillusionment, anger and pity (1916-18), and the post-war 'disenchanted' view of the late 1920s, when a boom in war books ran from 1928 to 1933.
notes.tip: The commonest Higher question here wants a clear thesis about change over time, supported by at least three named writers with dated works and a short, accurate quotation or close reference for each. Listing poems without saying what they show about attitudes loses marks.

notes.h: Early war voices: Brooke, Grenfell and McCrae
notes.b: At first many writers saw the war as a noble cause and death for one's country as a fulfilment. This mood drew on the cultural nationalism of the pre-war years.
points: Rupert Brooke's 1914 sonnets, published in 1915, include The Soldier, in which he imagines that if he dies, some corner of a foreign field will be 'for ever England'. They expressed idealism about dying for England.

Brooke died of blood poisoning on a hospital ship off the Greek island of Skyros on 23 April 1915, on the way to Gallipoli. He never saw major combat, but his early death made him celebrated as the ideal patriot.
Julian Grenfell (Into Battle, 1915; died of wounds in May 1915) and John McCrae, a Canadian army doctor (In Flanders Fields, written in 1915), wrote in a similar spirit.
Contemporaries preferred this patriotic verse, because it matched the mood of the time. The protest poets were read widely only after 1918.
notes.tip: Brooke is your example of early patriotism, but note that he died of illness in 1915 and never saw major combat. Contrast him with Owen and Sassoon, frontline officers who wrote in protest in 1917-18, and give dates.

notes.h: Protest and the soldier-poets: Sassoon, Rosenberg, Blunden and Gurney
notes.b: By 1917 officers who had survived the trenches began to write against the war. Siegfried Sassoon was the first to turn protest into a public act.
points: Siegfried Sassoon won the Military Cross in 1916, so when he protested he did so as a decorated officer, not a shirker.
In July 1917 he made a statement against the war, read out in the House of Commons and printed in The Times. It said the war was being 'deliberately prolonged' by those who had the power to end it.

Instead of a court martial he was sent to Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh in July 1917, after Robert Graves arranged a medical board. The army thus treated a decorated officer as ill rather than as a rebel.
His satire in The Old Huntsman (1917) and Counter-Attack (1918) attacked generals and the home front, which is why he is the model of the angry protest poet.
Other soldier-poets included Isaac Rosenberg (killed in April 1918), Edmund Blunden, who wrote Undertones of War (1928), and Ivor Gurney.
Sassoon survived the war and died in 1967, whereas Owen was killed in 1918.
notes.tip: For an ordinary-level paragraph on the war poets, give one contrast in attitude with dates: Brooke's idealism of 1914-15 against Sassoon's protest of 1917.

notes.h: Novels and memoirs: Barbusse, Jünger, Remarque, Graves and Brittain
notes.b: Prose writers carried the argument beyond the poets, from a French infantryman's view written during the war to German and British bestsellers of the late 1920s and early 1930s.
points: Henri Barbusse, who served as a private soldier, wrote Le Feu (Under Fire, 1916) during the war. It won the Prix Goncourt, showed the suffering of ordinary French infantrymen in the trenches and turned against the war.

Ernst Jünger's In Stahlgewittern (Storm of Steel, 1920) gave the viewpoint of a German officer who found meaning in combat. It contrasts with the protest writers, so war literature did not speak with one voice.

Erich Maria Remarque served on the Western Front and published Im Westen nichts Neues (All Quiet on the Western Front) in 1929. This post-war German novel showed a lost generation of young soldiers ruined by the war and became a worldwide bestseller. The Nazis burned it in 1933.

In the boom in war books of 1928-33, Robert Graves published the memoir Goodbye to All That (1929). Vera Brittain, a VAD nurse (Voluntary Aid Detachment, a wartime volunteer nurse) who lost her fiancé and brother, published Testament of Youth (1933), a woman's view.
Together, Remarque, Graves and Brittain shaped later memory of the war. This is why the post-war view is called disenchanted: it looked back on the war as a loss rather than a cause.
notes.tip: Do not mix the three novelists up: Barbusse is French and wrote in 1916, Remarque is German and published in 1929, and Jünger is German, wrote in 1920 and was positive about combat.

notes.h: War literature as historical evidence
notes.b: Historians use war literature as a source, but it is not a simple record of what soldiers thought. Its value and its limits both matter when you judge it.
points: Its strengths are eyewitness detail and strong feeling, so poems and memoirs convey the sights, sounds and emotions of the trenches in a way official reports do not.
Its limits are that the best-known writers were mostly educated officers and wrote for effect, so they may not speak for ordinary soldiers.

Many soldiers kept their belief that the war was justified. This is why revisionist historians such as Dan Todman, in The Great War: Myth and Memory (2005), argue that the poets' view became the 'myth' of a futile war which most soldiers did not share.
notes.tip: In an essay asking whether Owen made the most important contribution, compare him with at least two others (Brooke, Sassoon, Barbusse or Remarque). Naming the myth debate earns the evaluation marks.

notes.h: Key personality: Wilfred Owen
notes.b: Wilfred Owen fought as an officer and wrote as a witness for the men he led. He became the English poet most closely linked with the suffering of the war, yet almost nothing he wrote was published in his lifetime.
points: Owen was born on 18 March 1893 in Oswestry, Shropshire (in England, near the Welsh border, not in Wales), the eldest of four children of a railway worker. He was lay assistant to the vicar of Dunsden, Oxfordshire (1911-13), then taught English in Bordeaux from 1913.

He enlisted in the Artists Rifles in October 1915 and was commissioned in the Manchester Regiment in June 1916. In January 1917 he joined the 2nd Manchesters on the Somme sector, near Beaumont-Hamel, in severe winter conditions.

In March 1917 he suffered concussion. In April a shell blew him into the air and he lay for several days near the remains of a fellow officer. He was diagnosed with neurasthenia (shell shock, a nervous breakdown caused by the strain of bombardment).

He arrived at Craiglockhart War Hospital in Edinburgh in June 1917 and edited its magazine, The Hydra. He met Siegfried Sassoon there in August 1917, and Sassoon encouraged him. He met Robert Graves there in October 1917.

Between autumn 1917 and autumn 1918 he wrote or revised his best poems: Dulce et Decorum Est (drafted October 1917), Anthem for Doomed Youth (autumn 1917, opening 'What passing-bells for these who die as cattle?'), Strange Meeting, Futility and Exposure.
He was both participant and witness: an officer who fought, and who wrote on behalf of the men he led, so his poems carry the authority of experience.
notes.tip: For an essay on Owen as soldier and poet you need both halves with dates: enlistment 1915, the Somme sector 1917, shell shock, Craiglockhart, the Military Cross 1918 and death on 4 November 1918, plus the poems' themes and techniques.

notes.h: Key personality: Wilfred Owen, his poetry and reputation
notes.b: Owen's poems attack the idea that war is glorious, using the detail of what he had witnessed. His fame came after his death, and historians still debate what he represents.
points: Dulce et Decorum Est attacks 'The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori' (from Horace: it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country). Owen aims it at those at home who spread the idea.

His method was graphic detail of gas, mud and death, and pararhyme (matching consonants with a changed vowel instead of full rhyme, as in Strange Meeting), which sounds uneasy and unresolved. His draft preface says 'My subject is War, and the pity of War. The Poetry is in the pity.'
He returned to France in late summer 1918 and won the Military Cross for action at Joncourt on 1 October 1918. It was announced only after his death.
He was killed on 4 November 1918 crossing the Sambre-Oise canal near Ors, aged 25, a week before the armistice. The telegram reached his parents in Shrewsbury on 11 November 1918.
Owen was almost unknown in his lifetime, with only about five poems published. Poems (1920) was edited by Sassoon with Edith Sitwell, and Edmund Blunden produced a fuller edition in 1931.

Contemporaries: in the 1920s he was one of several war poets, and the public were drawn at first to Brooke. In 1936 W. B. Yeats excluded him from The Oxford Book of Modern Verse. Interest grew after the 1930s as pacifist feeling spread.

Later reputation: Benjamin Britten's War Requiem (1962), written for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral, sets nine Owen poems, and Owen became the best-known English poet of the war, taught in schools.

Historians: the biographers Jon Stallworthy (1974) and Dominic Hibberd (2002) stress his craft and development. Revisionists such as Dan Todman argue that the war poets' view became a myth of futile war not shared by most soldiers, and the poets' view came from an educated officer class.
notes.tip: For an ordinary-level paragraph on Owen, give the life in order with dates, plus two named poems and what each says about war. Do not just list poems: say what they show about attitudes.

notes.h: Church and state in Germany: the causes of the Kulturkampf
notes.b: The new German Reich was divided by religion. Chancellor Bismarck came to see the Catholic Church as a rival loyalty, and the conflict that followed was called the Kulturkampf.
points: The Reich, proclaimed in January 1871, was a Protestant-led state under Prussia. Protestants were about two-thirds of its people and Catholics about a third, living mainly in the south, the Rhineland and the Polish east. There is more on his wider policy in the notes on Bismarck.

In July 1870 the First Vatican Council (a gathering of the Church's bishops) declared papal infallibility, the doctrine that the Pope cannot err when defining Church teaching. Bismarck feared that German Catholics now owed their loyalty to Rome rather than to the Reich.

The Catholic Centre Party, founded in December 1870 and led by Ludwig Windthorst, defended Catholic interests. Bismarck called Catholics, socialists and national minorities 'Reichsfeinde' (enemies of the Reich) and saw the Centre as an enemy of the new state.
He also feared Polish Catholics in the east, because as a national minority whose faith set them apart from Protestant Prussia they seemed disloyal.

The National Liberals, his allies in the Reichstag, were anticlerical (opposed to Church influence in public life). They welcomed an attack on the Church as a defence of modern secular society, so the campaign had liberal support.
The conflict took its name in 1873 from Rudolf Virchow, a Progressive (liberal) deputy and scientist, who called it a Kulturkampf ('struggle for civilisation' or culture).
notes.tip: Marks go to causes: infallibility in 1870, Bismarck's idea of Catholics as enemies of the Reich, and the Centre Party. Explain why Bismarck began the Kulturkampf, not just what he did.

notes.h: The Kulturkampf: the laws of 1871-75
notes.b: Between 1871 and 1875 the Prussian and Reich governments passed laws that put schools, clergy and marriage under state control. The order matters, because each step escalated the conflict.
points: In July 1871 the Catholic department of the Prussian Ministry of Culture was abolished, and in December 1871 the Reich's Pulpit Law (Kanzelparagraph) made it an offence for clergy to criticise the state in sermons.

The School Supervision Law (Prussia, March 1872) put schools under state inspection, so the state rather than the clergy checked them. The Jesuit Law (July 1872) expelled the Jesuits (a Catholic religious order seen as loyal to the Pope) from Germany.
In May 1872 Bismarck told the Reichstag, 'We will not go to Canossa' (Nach Canossa gehen wir nicht), a vow not to give way to the papacy.

The May Laws of 1873 (Prussia), piloted by Adalbert Falk, Prussian Minister of Culture 1872-79, required priests to be educated at state universities and pass state exams, and made state approval necessary for church appointments.

Further laws followed. Civil marriage (a state ceremony instead of a church one) became compulsory in Prussia in 1874 and in the whole Reich in 1875. The Breadbasket Law of 1875 stopped state payments to the clergy, and most religious orders were dissolved in 1875.
Take care with names, because several laws share a label: these are the Prussian May Laws of 1873, not the Russian anti-Jewish May Laws of 1882 or the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878.
notes.tip: Give dated measures (1871 Pulpit Law, 1872 Jesuits and schools, 1873 May Laws, Falk) and always name the country when you mention a May Law. Narrating the laws without judging success or failure loses marks.

notes.h: The Kulturkampf: resistance and how it ended
notes.b: The laws did not break Catholic loyalty to the Church. They drove Catholics together, and within a few years Bismarck needed peace.
points: Pope Pius IX's encyclical Quod Nunquam (February 1875) declared the Prussian laws invalid. An encyclical is a formal letter from the Pope to the Church, known by its opening Latin words.
By 1876 every Prussian bishop was in prison or exile, and many parishes had no priest, because priests could not be appointed without state approval.

Catholics rallied behind the Centre under Ludwig Windthorst. In the Reichstag election of 1874 the Centre's vote roughly doubled, to about 1.4 million, and it won about 90 seats, making it the second-largest party.

Bismarck had reasons to end it. The policy had failed and strengthened the Centre. He needed Centre votes for the tariff law of 1879 and against the socialists, the new enemy (the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878), and he had broken with the National Liberals.
Pius IX died in February 1878 and Leo XIII was elected on 20 February 1878. The new pope was ready to negotiate, and Falk resigned in July 1879.
After negotiations with Leo XIII, mitigation laws (1880-83) and peace laws (1886-87) repealed or relaxed most of the measures.
Civil marriage, state school inspection and the Pulpit Law stayed. The Jesuit Law was relaxed in 1904 and repealed in 1917.
notes.tip: For why and how it ended, give the failure of the policy, the Centre's votes needed for tariffs and against socialists, Leo XIII's election, and the laws repealed by 1887. Do not say the Centre doubled its seats: its vote doubled, and its seats rose from about 60 to about 90.

notes.h: The Kulturkampf: results
notes.b: The Kulturkampf began as an attempt to subdue the Church and ended with the state giving way. Its results show the limits of Bismarck's power.
points: It was a political defeat for Bismarck, so he had to compromise with the Church and rely on the Centre Party he had set out to crush.
The Centre became a permanent, large party in the Reichstag, because the attack had united Catholics behind it.
Catholics felt alienated from the Protestant-led Reich, which left a lasting religious division in German politics.
Many people saw it as a model of state-church conflict and as a failure of liberalism, because liberals had welcomed state force against a religious minority.

notes.h: Church and state in Italy: the loss of Rome and the Roman Question
notes.b: In Italy the quarrel ran the other way round. The state was not attacking the Church; the Pope refused to accept a state that had taken his territory.
points: Until 1870 the Pope ruled central Italy as a temporal (worldly) ruler over the Papal States. The Kingdom of Italy, proclaimed in March 1861, took most of them, and Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870 (the breach at Porta Pia). Rome became the capital in 1871.
The First Vatican Council had declared papal infallibility only in July 1870, just before Rome was lost, so the Pope lost his territory at the moment he claimed greater spiritual authority.

The Law of Guarantees (May 1871) declared the Pope's person inviolable (he could not be attacked or arrested), gave him use of the Vatican, the Lateran and Castel Gandolfo, and offered a yearly payment.

Pius IX rejected the law and refused the payment, because accepting a law made by the Italian parliament would have meant recognising the state that had taken Rome. He described himself as a prisoner in the Vatican.

This unresolved dispute over the Pope's loss of Rome and his status was the Roman Question. The papacy's refusal to accept the loss divided Italians between the liberal, anticlerical state and the Catholic population.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the Law of Guarantees (Italy, 1871, rejected by the Pope) with the Lateran Treaty (1929, accepted). If asked why the Pope rejected the law, explain that he would not recognise the state that had taken Rome.

notes.h: Italy: non expedit and a divided country
notes.b: The Pope's refusal also shaped Italian politics, because he told Catholics to keep away from the state's elections. Catholics responded by building a separate world of their own.
points: Non expedit ('it is not expedient') was an instruction of 1868, confirmed in 1874, that Catholics should neither vote in nor stand for parliamentary elections.
As a result most Catholics stayed outside national politics, which left a narrow liberal ruling class in control of parliament.
Catholics remained active in local government and in social organisations: the Opera dei Congressi (founded 1874), Catholic Action, banks, newspapers and cooperatives.
The liberal state meanwhile expanded civil marriage and secular state schooling and closed religious houses, which deepened the divide.

Leo XIII kept the hard line on Rome. Pius X relaxed non expedit from 1905, and in the Gentiloni Pact of 1913 Catholic voters backed the liberal candidates of Giovanni Giolitti who promised to defend Catholic interests.

In January 1919, for example, Don Luigi Sturzo founded the Italian Popular Party (Partito Popolare Italiano). The Roman Question was settled only by the Lateran Treaty of 11 February 1929, beyond this period.

Compare the two countries. Germany's conflict was an attack by the state on the Church and was ended by compromise by 1887. Italy's was the Church's refusal to accept the state, and it lasted until 1929.
notes.tip: Non expedit (Italy: Catholics stay out of national elections) and the ralliement (France: Catholics accept the republic) are opposite advice to Catholics in two countries. Higher essays reward a comparison of Germany and Italy with a judgement.

notes.h: Church and state in France: background to Leo XIII and Dreyfus
notes.b: France's own quarrel between church and state is the setting for both Leo XIII's ralliement and the Dreyfus Affair, so its background has to be clear.
points: After defeat by Prussia in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870-71, France lost Alsace and part of Lorraine to Germany (Treaty of Frankfurt, 1871) and the Third Republic began in 1870. The army became the symbol of national pride and revenge.
The Third Republic was divided between republicans, who were often anticlerical (hostile to the Church's role in public life), and monarchist Catholics, who distrusted the republic.

The republic passed anticlerical laws: Jules Ferry's education laws of 1881-82 (free, compulsory, secular primary schooling), the Law of Associations (1901) and the Law of Separation of Church and State (December 1905). The Dreyfus Affair sped them up, because much of the Church sided against Dreyfus's defenders.

notes.h: Key personality: Leo XIII
notes.b: Leo XIII was pope from 1878 to 1903. After the confrontational reign of Pius IX he tried to renew the Church's relations with governments and the modern world.
points: Gioacchino (Vincenzo) Pecci was born on 2 March 1810 at Carpineto Romano. He was nuncio (the Pope's ambassador) to Belgium in 1843-46, Archbishop of Perugia 1846-78 and a cardinal from 1853, and was a diplomat and scholar.

He was elected pope on 20 February 1878, after Pius IX's reign (1846-78, marked by infallibility, the 'prisoner in the Vatican' stance and the Kulturkampf at its height). He remained pope until his death on 20 July 1903, aged 93.

He ended the Kulturkampf by negotiation with Bismarck in the 1880s, and the Centre Party's cooperation with the government helped to repeal most of the laws. In 1885 Bismarck referred the Caroline Islands dispute between Germany and Spain to him for arbitration.
He encouraged scholarship. His encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879) urged the study of Thomas Aquinas, and in 1881 he opened the Vatican archives to researchers.
In April 1888 the Holy Office (a Vatican department) issued a decree condemning the Plan of Campaign and boycotting in Ireland, which gives his papacy an Irish link.
He refused to accept the loss of the Papal States and kept the 'prisoner in the Vatican' stance and non expedit in Italy, so the Roman Question remained open. He was also conservative on doctrine.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the popes: Pius IX (1846-78: infallibility, 'prisoner in the Vatican', Kulturkampf at its height), Leo XIII (1878-1903: peace with Bismarck, Rerum Novarum, ralliement), Pius X (1903-14: relaxed non expedit) and Pius XI (Lateran Treaty 1929, Quadragesimo Anno).

notes.h: Key personality: Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum and the ralliement
notes.b: Leo XIII is best known for two initiatives, a statement on workers' rights and a call for French Catholics to accept the republic. Both show how he tried to move the papacy from lost territory to moral influence.
points: Rerum Novarum (15 May 1891), an encyclical on 'the condition of the working classes' (the rights and duties of capital and labour), answered the social question in general terms. It rejected socialism and class war and defended private property.

It upheld the right of workers to a just wage, decent conditions and trade unions, and called on states to protect workers and the poor. It thus offered Catholics a route between socialism and unregulated capitalism.

Rerum Novarum became the foundation of modern Catholic social teaching and encouraged Catholic trade unions and Christian democratic parties in Germany, Belgium, Italy and elsewhere. Pius XI marked its fortieth anniversary with Quadragesimo Anno (1931), which shows its lasting influence.

The ralliement ('rallying') of 1890-92 urged French Catholics to accept the republic and work within it. It began with Cardinal Lavigerie's toast to the republic at Algiers in November 1890 and was set out in the encyclical Au milieu des sollicitudes (February 1892).

Monarchist Catholics largely refused. The Dreyfus Affair and the anticlerical laws of the early 1900s, ending in the 1905 separation of church and state, wrecked the policy, because much of the Church sided with the anti-Dreyfusards.

Contemporaries: governments and many workers respected him as a moderate reformer. Conservative Catholics distrusted his accommodation with republics, and socialists opposed his rejection of socialism.

Historians regard him as the first modern pope, who moved the papacy from lost temporal power to moral and social influence. Critics regard Rerum Novarum as cautious and paternalist, and the ralliement as a failure.
notes.tip: For an ordinary paragraph give dated, specific statements: elected 1878, ended the Kulturkampf, Aeterni Patris 1879, Rerum Novarum 1891 with its main points (property, just wage, unions, no socialism), the ralliement, died 1903. For higher essays, judge achievements against limits.

notes.h: Anti-Semitism: meaning and causes
notes.b: Anti-Semitism is hostility to Jews as a people. After 1870 older religious prejudice was joined by political and racial forms, which is why it matters in this period.
points: Anti-Jewish prejudice was old in Europe and had been mainly religious. After 1870 political and racial anti-Semitism spread. Wilhelm Marr popularised the word 'anti-Semitism' and founded the League of Antisemites in 1879; the term existed before him.
Economic depression from the stock-market crash of 1873 made many people resent Jewish success in finance, trade and the professions, and look for scapegoats.

Nationalism that defined the nation by blood or religion treated Jews as outsiders, and pseudo-scientific race theory (claims, without scientific basis, that humans divide into biologically different races) gave prejudice a modern look.
Jews were blamed at once for modernity, capitalism and socialism, so anti-Semites of very different politics could all find a target.
notes.tip: Examiners may ask you to explain anti-Semitism as a key concept: give its religious, economic, racial and political forms, with an example from France or Russia for each country.

notes.h: Anti-Semitism in France: Drumont and the arrest of Dreyfus
notes.b: French Jews were a small, assimilated minority, yet after 1870 nationalists and journalists made them scapegoats. The Dreyfus Affair grew out of this mood.
points: French Jews had been full citizens since 1791. Defeat in 1870-71, the Panama Canal Company scandal of 1892 and economic fears gave anti-Semites targets, and nationalists blamed Jews and Freemasons for the country's weakness.
Édouard Drumont's La France juive (1886) was a bestseller that portrayed Jews as a threat to France. In 1892 he founded the newspaper La Libre Parole to carry on the campaign.

Captain Alfred Dreyfus, born in Mulhouse, Alsace, in 1859, was a Jewish artillery officer on the General Staff. Arrested on 15 October 1894, he was accused of passing secrets to Germany; the evidence was a memorandum, the bordereau.

A court martial sitting in closed session convicted him in December 1894, after the judges were shown a secret file not given to the defence. He was publicly degraded on 5 January 1895 and sent to Devil's Island in French Guiana.
notes.tip: Describe the 1894 trial accurately: it sat in closed session and the judges saw a secret file that the defence did not. Keep the cast distinct: Dreyfus (accused), Esterhazy (real author), Picquart, Henry (forger), Zola and Drumont.

notes.h: The Dreyfus Affair: the truth, J'accuse and a divided France
notes.b: The case became an Affair when evidence of Dreyfus's innocence emerged and the army refused to admit its mistake. Public opinion then split France in two.
points: In 1896 Lieutenant-Colonel Georges Picquart, head of army intelligence, identified Major Ferdinand Walsin-Esterhazy as the real author of the bordereau. The army suppressed this: Picquart was posted to Tunisia, and Esterhazy was acquitted by court martial on 11 January 1898.

On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published the open letter 'J'accuse...!' to President Félix Faure in the newspaper L'Aurore (its editor Georges Clemenceau chose the headline), accusing the army of covering up the truth. Zola was convicted of libel in February and fled to England in July 1898.

France divided. Dreyfusards, who defended Dreyfus, included Zola, Clemenceau, the socialist leader Jean Jaurès, many republicans and intellectuals, and the League of the Rights of Man (founded 1898). Anti-Dreyfusards included army leaders, much of the Catholic press, nationalists, monarchists and anti-Semitic leagues.
Anti-Jewish riots broke out in French cities and in Algeria in 1898, which shows how far the prejudice had spread.
In August 1898 the forgery by Lieutenant-Colonel Henry was exposed, and he cut his throat in prison.
A second court martial at Rennes (August-September 1899) again found Dreyfus guilty, 'with extenuating circumstances', and gave him ten years. President Émile Loubet pardoned him in September 1899.
In July 1906 the Cour de cassation (France's highest appeal court) quashed the Rennes verdict, and Dreyfus was reinstated in the army as a major and given the Legion of Honour.
notes.tip: Learn the dates in order: arrest 1894, J'accuse 1898, Rennes and pardon 1899, rehabilitation 1906. A pardon (1899) is not an acquittal (1906).

notes.h: The Dreyfus Affair: results and Zionism
notes.b: The Affair changed French politics, and it also had an effect beyond France through the birth of political Zionism.
points: It was a republican victory and ended in justice for one man, because the courts and a free press could finally correct the army's error.

It discredited the army, whose leaders had covered up the truth, and the Church, much of whose press had sided with the anti-Dreyfusards. It led to the anticlerical laws of the early 1900s and the 1905 separation of church and state.
A new nationalist right emerged, such as Action Française (founded 1899), and anti-Semitism survived the Affair.
Theodor Herzl reported on the case for the Vienna Neue Freie Presse and later said it convinced him that Jews needed a state of their own. Historians debate how much it mattered.
Herzl published Der Judenstaat (The Jewish State) in 1896, and the First Zionist Congress, the first meeting of the movement for a Jewish national home (Zionism), met at Basel in August 1897.
notes.tip: Examiners ask what the Affair changed and why it divided France: the army and Church discredited, secular laws, a new nationalist right and surviving anti-Semitism.

notes.h: Anti-Semitism in Russia: the Pale and the pogroms of 1881-82
notes.b: In the Russian Empire anti-Jewish prejudice was backed by the state. Laws confined Jews and kept many poor, and violent attacks on them were tolerated.
points: The Empire was a tsarist autocracy (rule by a tsar with unlimited power) with the Orthodox Church as the state church and a policy of Russification (imposing Russian language and control on minorities).
About five million Jews lived in the Empire in the late 1800s (the 1897 census), the largest Jewish population in the world. Many were poor artisans and traders.
Most were confined to the Pale of Settlement, the western provinces where Jews were allowed to live, created in 1791 under Catherine the Great and abolished in 1917.

Alexander II was assassinated on 13 March 1881 (1 March in the Russian calendar), and rumours blamed Jews. Pogroms (violent attacks on Jewish communities) began at Elizavetgrad in April 1881 and spread across the south, including Kiev and Odessa, continuing to 1884.
Officials were slow to act or blamed the victims, so the violence spread unchecked.

The May Laws (Temporary Regulations) of May 1882 banned new Jewish settlement in rural areas and restricted Jews from acquiring land and property outside towns. Though called temporary, they remained in force until 1917.
notes.tip: Name the country whenever you say May Laws: the Russian May Laws of 1882 are anti-Jewish, unlike the Prussian May Laws of 1873. Also keep the pogroms apart: 1881-82, Kishinev 1903 and 1905.

notes.h: Official anti-Semitism, Kishinev and the Black Hundreds
notes.b: Under Alexander III and Nicholas II discrimination became settled government policy, and violence continued.
points: From 1887 quotas (numerus clausus) limited the number of Jewish students in secondary schools and universities. About 20,000 Jews were expelled from Moscow in 1891-92, and there were limits on the professions.

Konstantin Pobedonostsev, Over-Procurator of the Holy Synod (the state official in charge of the Orthodox Church) from 1880 to 1905 and tutor and adviser to Alexander III and Nicholas II, supported discrimination and Russification. Alexander III and Nicholas II were themselves personally hostile to Jews.
Some clergy spread anti-Jewish propaganda. From 1905 the Union of the Russian People, whose street gangs were called the Black Hundreds, did the same.

The Kishinev pogrom in Bessarabia, at Easter on 6-7 April 1903 (19-20 April in the Western calendar), killed about 49 Jews and injured hundreds, and caused international outrage. Hayim Nahman Bialik wrote his poem 'In the City of Slaughter' in response.
More pogroms followed in 1905-06 during the revolution, after the October Manifesto of 1905, and were worst in Odessa.
For example, in the Beilis case Menahem Mendel Beilis, a Kiev Jew, was arrested in 1911 and tried for 'ritual murder' (the false claim that Jews murder for religious rites). He was acquitted in 1913.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why the Russian state encouraged anti-Semitism (scapegoating, Russification, Orthodox nationalism) and what resulted: emigration, Jews turning to revolution, and international outrage.

notes.h: The Protocols, Jewish responses and the end of the system
notes.b: Forged propaganda spread the myth of a Jewish plot, while Jews responded by leaving, organising or joining revolution. The legal system ended only in 1917.
points: The Protocols of the Elders of Zion, which claimed a Jewish plot to dominate the world, was forged in Russia. It was first serialised in the St Petersburg paper Znamya in 1903 and appeared in book form in 1905 (Sergei Nilus).
In 1921 The Times showed that it was plagiarised from Maurice Joly's satire of Napoleon III (1864). It spread worldwide after 1917.
About two million Jews left the Russian Empire between 1881 and 1914, most to the USA and others to Britain and Palestine, because persecution and poverty made life there hard.

The General Jewish Labour Bund, a Jewish socialist party, was founded in Vilna in 1897. Zionism, the movement for a Jewish national home, was separate: it was a national movement, not a socialist one.
Many young Jews also joined revolutionary parties, so persecution pushed some towards revolution as well as emigration.
The Provisional Government removed all legal restrictions on Jews in March and April 1917, ending the Pale and the legal disabilities. Pogroms returned in the civil war.
notes.tip: For Russia, tie each event to its date: the Pale (1791), 1881 pogroms, May Laws 1882, Kishinev 1903, the Protocols, and emigration of about two million between 1881 and 1914.

notes.h: Assessment: culture, faith and exclusion
notes.b: Examiners reward judgement, so each theme from national identity to anti-Semitism needs both a success and a limit. Each point pairs them.
points: National identity in the arts: it liberated peoples without a state, such as the Czechs, Finns and Norwegians, but in Germany and Britain it fed imperial pride, exclusive nationalism and the war spirit of 1914.

War literature: 1914-15 patriotism against 1917-18 protest. Contemporaries preferred Brooke, later generations Owen and Sassoon. The literature is valuable as eyewitness evidence, but the 'myth' argument reminds us that most soldiers did not share the protest view.
Kulturkampf: a success in state control of schools and marriage, but a political failure, because the Centre was strengthened and Bismarck was forced to compromise.
Italy: the liberal state survived and kept Rome, but there was a lasting split from Catholic Italy until 1929.
Leo XIII: achievements in ending the Kulturkampf, Rerum Novarum and papal prestige, against limits in the failed ralliement and the unresolved Roman Question.

Anti-Semitism compared: in France a popular and press movement that a republic finally defeated in the courts, giving justice to Dreyfus. In Russia a state-backed policy of laws and tolerated violence that drove mass emigration. Prejudice survived in both.
notes.tip: For comparing states, contrast the Kulturkampf, the Roman Question and France's secular laws with the treatment of Jews in France and Russia, and say which state was most and least successful.

keyTerms.definition: Hostility towards or discrimination against Jews, which took political, legal and violent forms in France and Russia between 1871 and 1914.
Loyalty to the nation and belief that it should be strong and self-governing, expressed in music, literature, monuments and religion.
Bismarck's conflict with the Catholic Church in Germany, 1871-87, to bring schools, marriage and clergy under state control.
The Catholic party founded in Germany in 1870, which defended the Church and grew stronger during the Kulturkampf.
The dispute between the Italian state and the papacy after Italy seized Rome in 1870, unresolved until the Lateran Treaties of 1929.
The papal instruction forbidding Italian Catholics to vote in or stand for national elections.
Leo XIII's policy of urging French Catholics to accept the Third Republic.
Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical on the condition of the working classes, defending a just wage and trade unions while rejecting socialism.
A violent mob attack on Jewish communities, tolerated or encouraged by officials, as in Russia in 1881-82 and 1903.
The western region of the Russian Empire to which most Jews were confined by law from 1791 to 1917.

A tone poem of 1899-1900 that became a symbol of Finnish national feeling under Russian rule.
Brooke's 1914 sonnets expressed idealism; Owen's poems of 1917-18 expressed disillusionment and pity.
At Craiglockhart War Hospital near Edinburgh in August 1917.
Born 1893, at Craiglockhart 1917, Military Cross October 1918, killed 4 November 1918.

Expulsion of the Jesuits (1872), state control of schools (1872), and the May Laws of 1873 on the training and appointment of priests.

factCards.term: Why did Bismarck end the Kulturkampf?
factCards.definition: He needed the Centre Party against socialists and for tariffs, and the policy had strengthened Catholic unity.
Italian law giving the Pope the Vatican and an income; Pius IX rejected it and called himself a prisoner.
Ended the Kulturkampf, issued Rerum Novarum in 1891, and promoted the ralliement in France.
It upheld private property but also workers' right to a just wage and to form unions, and rejected socialism and class war.
Arrest in October 1894, Zola's J'accuse in January 1898, pardon in 1899 and exoneration in 1906.
A pogrom in April 1903 in which 49 Jews were killed, causing international outrage.

factCards.term: The Protocols of the Elders of Zion
factCards.definition: A forged text, first published in Russia in 1903, claiming a Jewish plot for world domination.
